passage: Sit down, beta. Mahima aunty will tell you about my second year at the packaging firm. I was twenty-four, and my manager Chandrika slid a delivery form across her desk and said, "Just date it the twenty-eighth, the truck was basically there." The truck had reached on the second. My hands went cold. Chandrika had helped me get that job, and I thought of my loan. So I signed. Six weeks later an auditor asked for the gate records, and the mismatch carried my signature. Chandrika said, "You should have told me no." I still hear that. If I could go back, I would ask for the order in writing, or say I am not comfortable, and go to the head of accounts if pushed. Instead I learned it late, and at a cost.

qa.q: When did the truck actually arrive?
qa.a: The truck had reached on the second.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when the form was slid across the desk?
qa.a: Frightened and torn: Mahima's hands went cold and the thought of the loan pressed on the decision.

qa.q: What choice could Mahima have made at the desk instead of signing?
qa.a: Mahima could have asked for the order in writing, said she was not comfortable, or gone to the head of accounts if pushed.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt when the auditor found the mismatch?
qa.a: Probably worried and defensive, since Chandrika answered by saying, "You should have told me no."

grounding: Illustrates a junior employee asked by a superior to backdate a form, torn between loyalty, fear and conscience, who complies and regrets it.

passage: The power went off at 4:10, and the bank's payment window shut at five. Ankita's laptop was on its last battery when Deepak leaned over her shoulder. "Skip the second approval and release all twelve. I will answer for it." She knew the rule existed for a reason. Deepak had trained her, and he had always covered for her mistakes. Her stomach tightened. She typed, "Can we ask Ms Iyer for two minutes?" but Deepak was already pointing at the clock. She clicked release. On Monday one vendor turned out to be paid twice, and the recovery took three weeks of emails. In the meeting Deepak said the process had failed. Ankita said nothing, and thought about the question she had typed and never sent.

qa.q: How many payments did Deepak tell Ankita to release?
qa.a: Deepak told Ankita to release all twelve.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she looked from the clock to Deepak?
qa.a: Torn between loyalty and fear, with her stomach tightening and her conscience nagging.

qa.q: What could Ankita have done differently at that moment?
qa.a: Send the question to Ms Iyer or insist on the second approval, even with the clock running.

qa.q: How might Deepak see what happened afterwards?
qa.a: Deepak said the process had failed, which suggests he was defensive and stressed and did not name his own part.

grounding: Illustrates a junior employee ordered to skip a required check who complies out of loyalty and fear and later regrets it.

passage: Mentor's note, Kiran. Tushar was quiet at Thursday's check-in and, when I asked, said he had watched the shift lead sign the weekly stock-count sheet without walking the shelves. "It is probably fine," he said twice, and looked at the table. He said it was not his place and that he feared being labelled a complainer in his first year. I did not tell him what to do. I asked what question he could ask that would be true and not an accusation. He came up with, "Did I miss when the shelf count was done?" I noted that he sounded relieved to say it aloud. We agreed he would try it on Monday and tell me how it went.

qa.q: How many times did Tushar say "It is probably fine"?
qa.a: Tushar said it twice.

qa.q: What was Tushar afraid of?
qa.a: Being labelled a complainer in his first year, and he was unsure whether it was his place.

qa.q: What question did Tushar come up with, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: He came up with "Did I miss when the shelf count was done?", which is true and not an accusation.

qa.q: How might the shift lead react to a calm question about the count?
qa.a: Perhaps caught off guard, but the question leaves room to answer without being accused, and it could prompt the count to be done.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker who sees a questionable practice, doubts whether it is their business and fears the cost of speaking up.

passage:
Tuesday, 11:50 p.m. Saw it again today. Sahil filled in his site-visit sheet for the whole week and put down two visits on days he was in the office; I know because I sat next to him. It is not my job to police anyone, is it? And what if I have the dates wrong? Sahil is well liked and I am still on probation. So I made tea, said nothing and sat with my laptop feeling small. It has been three weeks. Riya from accounts asked whether the sheets looked normal and I said, "Seems so." I am writing this down because I wish I had simply asked, "Hey, did I get the dates wrong for those two sites?" Maybe tomorrow. Maybe.
Dhruv

qa.q: How many site visits did Dhruv notice on Sahil's sheet that did not match?
qa.a: Dhruv noticed two visits on days Sahil was in the office.

qa.q: What is Dhruv worried about?
qa.a: Being wrong about the dates and the cost of speaking up while still on probation, so Dhruv feels small and uneasy.

qa.q: What could Dhruv say to Sahil?
qa.a: Ask, "Did I get the dates wrong for those two sites?" as a question and not an accusation.

qa.q: How might Sahil react to that question?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, then check the dates and correct them, or feel defensive; the question leaves a way to answer without an accusation.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker who notices a questionable practice, stays silent from doubt and fear, and wishes to have asked a question.

passage: Mentor's note, Alka. Jasleen came to me with a folder: a printed invoice showing 400 units and the delivery slip showing 340, with dates pencilled in the margin. She had already asked her line manager in person, "Can you help me understand why these two do not match?" The manager said, "I will look into it," and two weeks later nothing had moved. I asked what she wanted to do. She wrote a short email to the compliance officer with the facts only, no guesses about anyone's motives, and attached her folder. The next morning the officer replied, thanked her, said the matter would be reviewed and asked her to keep her notes safe. I noted that she stayed calm and never accused anyone.

qa.q: How many units did the invoice show, compared with the delivery slip?
qa.a: The invoice showed 400 units and the delivery slip showed 340.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's decision to stick to the facts suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: She was calm and careful, wanting to be fair and worried about accusing wrongly.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do when her line manager's promise led nowhere?
qa.a: She emailed the compliance officer with the facts only and attached her folder.

qa.q: How might the compliance officer see Jasleen's email?
qa.a: As a clear, fair report worth acting on, since the officer thanked Jasleen the next morning, promised a review and asked her to keep her notes safe.

grounding: Illustrates a person who documents facts, asks the direct manager first and then uses an official channel when it is ignored.

passage:
Wednesday night. Noticed three donation receipts in the March file of the community library with no matching deposit slips. Could be paperwork lag. Before saying anything, I wrote it all on one page: receipt numbers, dates, amounts, and which slips I had checked. Just facts. At four I asked Madhav, "Could you help me understand where the deposit slips for these three are? I might be missing a file." He looked at the page, said, "Give me till Friday, I will check," and took a photo of it. I do not think he was annoyed. I saved a copy in my own folder. If Friday comes and nothing changes, the next step is an email to the trustees, using the same page. Breathing easier now. It felt less like an accusation and more like a question.
Sangeeta

qa.q: How many receipts lacked deposit slips?
qa.a: Three donation receipts had no matching deposit slips.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling after asking Madhav?
qa.a: Calmer and relieved, since it felt less like an accusation and more like a question.

qa.q: What is the next step if nothing changes by Friday?
qa.a: Email the trustees, using the same page of facts.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt about being asked?
qa.a: Possibly surprised but not annoyed, since he took a photo of the page and asked for until Friday, which suggests he took it seriously. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a person who writes down facts, asks the person directly with a question first, and plans an official channel if ignored.

passage: On Monday, Kunal opened the stock sheet he had sent to Kalyani, a client who ran a small furniture shop, and saw that two columns had swapped, so the prices on it were wrong. His first thought was to fix it quietly and hope she had not used it. On Tuesday he rang her instead. "The sheet I sent has an error. Please do not use it for orders. I can send a corrected one by Thursday noon, and I will add a checking step before every future file." There was a pause. "Thank you for telling me now," Kalyani said. On Friday the corrected sheet had gone out, and Kalyani had placed her orders using it. She asked Kunal to take on the next project.

qa.q: What was wrong with the stock sheet?
qa.a: Two columns had swapped, so the prices on it were wrong.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling on Monday when he first saw the swapped columns?
qa.a: Worried and tempted to hide it, since his first thought was to fix it quietly and hope she had not used it.

qa.q: Why was it better to phone Kalyani on Tuesday?
qa.a: Because Kalyani could avoid orders at the wrong prices, and the corrected sheet and the checking step gave her a real alternative.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel after that call?
qa.a: Grateful and reassured that Kunal told her early, which is why she gave him the next project.

grounding: Illustrates a person who tells a client plainly what went wrong and offers a real fix, so the short-term discomfort stays small.

passage: Chinmay uncle here, so listen. When I was twenty-five and painting signboards, Rafiq, who ran the sweet shop by the bus stand, ordered a big board for his shop's opening on Sunday. By Thursday the paint was still wet and two letters were crooked. I could have hurried and delivered a smudged board. Instead I walked to his shop and said, "It will not be right by Sunday. I can give you a plain banner for the opening, and the proper board on Wednesday, at no extra charge." Rafiq's face fell. He shouted a little. Then he took the banner. On Wednesday he stood back from the new board, and that month he sent three neighbours to me. That Sunday was uncomfortable, but a smudged board would have been worse.

qa.q: What did Chinmay offer Rafiq for the opening on Sunday?
qa.a: Chinmay offered a plain banner for the opening and the proper board on Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel when told the board would not be ready?
qa.a: Disappointed and angry, since his face fell and he shouted a little.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make on Thursday that mattered?
qa.a: Chinmay walked to the shop and told Rafiq honestly, with a real alternative, instead of delivering a smudged board.

qa.q: How might the young Chinmay have seen that uncomfortable Sunday afterwards?
qa.a: Chinmay saw it as a price worth paying, since a smudged board would have been worse and the honest word led Rafiq to send three neighbours.

grounding: Illustrates a person under pressure who says plainly what cannot be done and offers a real alternative, which builds trust.
